blocks.text: The otoscope is a diagnostic instrument used to examine the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane (eardrum). It is commonly tested in medicine, pediatrics, emergency medicine and ENT OSCE stations.
Your goal is to identify the instrument, demonstrate correct ear examination, recognise normal and abnormal findings, and explain its limitations and safety precautions.
Name: Otoscope.
Classification: Diagnostic instrument used for examination of the ear.
Main types:
A. Conventional direct otoscope
A handheld device with a light source, magnifying lens and detachable ear speculum. It is the common bedside instrument.
B. Pneumatic otoscope
An otoscope with an attachment that allows controlled changes in pressure in the ear canal to assess tympanic membrane mobility. It is useful when evaluating middle-ear effusion.
C. Video otoscope
Uses a camera to display the ear canal and tympanic membrane on a screen, allowing documentation and demonstration of findings.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is an otoscope, a diagnostic instrument used to examine the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane. It consists of a handle, illumination system, viewing lens and detachable ear speculum.”

items.text: Portable: easy to carry during ward rounds and bedside examinations.
Rapid assessment: helps identify common causes of ear pain, discharge and hearing problems.
Magnification: allows detailed inspection of the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane.
Relatively inexpensive: widely available in primary care, emergency departments and hospitals.
Useful in children: enables assessment for acute otitis media and other ear conditions.
Pneumatic capability: certain models assess tympanic membrane mobility, helping identify middle-ear effusion.
Improved communication: video otoscopes can display findings to patients, caregivers or trainees.
Limited field of view: only the visible portion of the ear canal and tympanic membrane can be examined.
Cerumen obstruction: impacted wax may prevent adequate visualisation.
Patient movement: particularly in infants and young children, movement can make examination difficult.
Narrow or swollen canal: may prevent insertion of an appropriately sized speculum.
Operator dependence: correct positioning and interpretation require practice.
Poor visibility: discharge, debris, blood or canal oedema may obscure the tympanic membrane.
Limited diagnostic scope: otoscopy alone cannot reliably establish the type or severity of every hearing disorder.
No routine assessment of hearing thresholds: audiometry is required when quantitative hearing assessment is indicated.

blocks.text: Examiner tip: If you cannot see the tympanic membrane, say so. Do not report it as normal simply because no abnormality is visible.

blocks.text: Suspected perforation or ear trauma: examine gently, avoid unnecessary pressure and do not perform pneumatic otoscopy if a perforation or other contraindication is suspected.
Suspected button battery: an ear-canal button battery is an emergency. Arrange immediate specialist removal; do not irrigate or delay treatment.
Foreign bodies: avoid repeated blind attempts at removal, particularly when the object is impacted, sharp, a battery, or adjacent to the tympanic membrane.

Ear irrigation: do not irrigate if there is a known or suspected tympanic membrane perforation, previous relevant ear surgery, or a suspected button battery. Other contraindications and precautions must also be considered.
Infection control: use a new disposable speculum for each patient or appropriately reprocess reusable equipment. Do not insert the speculum farther than necessary.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use an otoscope — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

content_groups.group_title: Step 1: Introduce yourself and obtain consent

blocks.text: “Hello, I am going to examine your ears using an otoscope. I will gently place a small speculum at the entrance of each ear canal so I can examine the canal and eardrum. You may feel some pressure, but please tell me if you experience pain.”
Confirm the patient's identity, obtain consent and perform hand hygiene.

items.text: Sit the adult comfortably with the head supported.
For a child, use a safe, comfortable position with the caregiver's assistance if appropriate.
Explain the procedure in age-appropriate language.
Ensure adequate lighting.

blocks.text: Before inserting the otoscope, examine both pinnae and the surrounding skin.

items.text: Redness or swelling.

blocks.text: If clinically indicated, examine the tragus and mastoid area for tenderness. Significant postauricular swelling or tenderness, especially with a displaced pinna and systemic illness, raises concern for mastoiditis.
Choose the largest speculum that fits comfortably without force. Attach it securely to the otoscope.
Check that the light and viewing lens work properly.
Hold the otoscope like a pen, with your hand supported against the patient's head. This stabilises the instrument and reduces the risk of injury if the patient moves suddenly.
Adults and older children
Gently pull the pinna upwards and backwards to straighten the canal.
Infants and young children
Gently pull the pinna downwards and backwards, adjusting the technique to the child's age and anatomy.
The exact technique depends on age and ear anatomy. The essential principle is to straighten the canal gently without causing pain.

items.text: Insert the speculum slowly and under direct visual guidance.
Follow the natural direction of the ear canal.
Avoid force and avoid pushing against the canal walls.
Keep your hand braced against the patient's head.
Stop if there is significant pain, resistance or unexpected movement.

blocks.text: Never insert the speculum blindly or deeply.

blocks.text: Do not diagnose acute otitis media from redness alone. A bulging tympanic membrane, acute symptoms and evidence of middle-ear effusion are more diagnostically useful.
If a pneumatic otoscope is available and it is safe to use, apply gentle, controlled pressure changes while observing the tympanic membrane.

blocks.text: Repeat the examination on the other side using the same systematic approach. Compare the findings.
Withdraw the speculum gently, remove or dispose of it appropriately, clean the instrument as required and perform hand hygiene.
Thank the patient and report the findings, including any limitations in visualisation.

Routine otoscopy is generally safe, but certain conditions require modification or specialist assessment.

items.text: W — Wax impaction.
B — Bulging tympanic membrane: consider acute otitis media.
P — Perforation.

blocks.text: **Mnemonic 3: Safe otoscopy — G-E-N-T-L-E**

items.text: G — Gain consent.
E — Examine the external ear first.
N — Note the patient's age and canal anatomy.
T — Take the largest comfortable speculum.
L — Lock your hand against the patient's head for stability.
E — Examine gently and stop if unsafe.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is an otoscope used for?
Answer: It is used to examine the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane.
Q2. How do you straighten the ear canal in an adult?
Answer: Gently pull the pinna upwards and backwards.
Q3. How does this differ in a young infant?
Answer: Gently pull the pinna downwards and backwards to help straighten the canal.
Q4. What does a normal tympanic membrane look like?
Answer: It is generally pearly grey or translucent, intact and without significant bulging, retraction or inflammation.
Q5. What is the most characteristic otoscopic finding in acute otitis media?
Answer: A bulging tympanic membrane in a patient with compatible acute symptoms and evidence of middle-ear effusion. Redness alone is not sufficient.
Q6. What is the difference between otitis externa and otitis media?

Answer: Otitis externa primarily affects the external auditory canal, often causing canal oedema and pain on tragal or pinna manipulation. Otitis media affects the middle ear and may produce a bulging tympanic membrane and middle-ear effusion.
Q7. What is pneumatic otoscopy?
Answer: It uses controlled pressure changes to assess tympanic membrane mobility. Reduced mobility can suggest middle-ear effusion or other middle-ear pathology.
Q8. What should you do if you cannot see the tympanic membrane because of wax?
Answer: Document that visualisation is inadequate, assess whether wax removal is appropriate and safe, and arrange further examination if necessary. Do not label the tympanic membrane normal.
Q9. Why is a button battery in the ear an emergency?
Answer: It can cause rapid tissue injury and necrosis. It requires immediate emergency removal, and irrigation should be avoided.
Q10. What is the purpose of bracing your hand against the patient's head?
Answer: It stabilises the instrument and reduces the risk of injury if the patient moves suddenly.
Q11. What does a retracted tympanic membrane suggest?
Answer: It may indicate negative middle-ear pressure, commonly associated with Eustachian tube dysfunction.
Q12. Can otoscopy alone assess hearing accurately?
Answer: No. Otoscopy identifies visible abnormalities, but hearing thresholds require appropriate hearing assessment, such as audiometry when indicated.
Mistake: Forgetting to inspect the pinna
Examine the external ear before inserting the speculum. Look for swelling, lesions, trauma and discharge.
Mistake: Using the wrong pinna traction
Use upward-and-backward traction in adults and downward-and-backward traction in young infants.
Mistake: Inserting the speculum too deeply or forcefully
Choose an appropriate speculum, brace your hand and proceed under direct vision. Stop if the patient experiences significant pain or moves unexpectedly.
Mistake: Calling a red tympanic membrane acute otitis media
Look for bulging, effusion and compatible acute symptoms. Crying and irritation can also cause tympanic membrane redness.
Mistake: Forgetting to examine the other ear
Compare both ears and document any differences.
Examiner tip: Describe the canal and membrane separately
A structured report shows that you can distinguish external ear disease from middle-ear pathology.
